newsitem.title: GERMANY: Cuban nickel output set to rise substantially.
newsitem.headline: Cuban nickel output set to rise substantially.

text.p: Nickel mine production in Cuba is set to rise substantially in 1997 as the country upgrades its plants in a bid to boost hard currency earnings, delegates at a stainless steel industry conference said on Wednesday.

"Cuba offers the organisation and motivation to make the nickel industry attractive to foreign investors," Henk Verhoek, chief executive officer of Niref, the Netherlands-based European sales agents for Cubaniquel, told Reuters.
"The Cubans need to employ new technology and to cut costs ... sales of their products are very successful."
Verhoek put refined nickel production at the country's Nicaro plant in 1997 at 13,000 tonnes and at the Punta Gorda plant at 25,000 tonnes.

Cuba's third plant, Moa (Bay) Nickel SA, was set to produce 26,000-27,000 tonnes of a 55/5 pct nickel-cobalt sulphide which it sells to Sherritt International Corp for refining in Saskatchewan, Canada, he added.

Figures from German researcher Heinz Pariser Alloy Metals & Steel showed Nicaro last year produced 10,701 tonnes and Punta Gorda a record 16,923 tonnes, while Moa SA's nickel/cobalt product amounted to 26,034 tonnes.
The figures, gathered at a recent seminar organised at Guardalavaca in Cuba by Pariser's firm, had the approval of Cuban authorities.

Installed capacity at the three plants was listed by Heinz Pariser as follows -- Nicaro (also known as Cmdte Rene Ramos Latour) 17,000 tonnes, Punta Gorda (also known as Cmdte Ernesto Che Guevara) 30,000 tonnes and Moa 26,000 tonnes.
Moa Nickel, also known as Pedro Sotto Alba, slightly exceeded its originally designed capacity, Pariser's data showed, confirming official Cuban statements last November.
The figures also included an estimate of identified reserves of nickel laterites at 1.08 billion tonnes, of which 63 percent were classified as proven reserves and 37 percent as possible reserves.
Verhoek said Cuba had nickel reserves potentially lasting for 200 years of production in its north-eastern mining region.

Pariser, who was at the Metal Bulletin conference to talk about flat stainless products, said in an interview with Reuters that nickel had been identified by the government as a key industry and it appeared well managed.
"The plants appear to have some problems but they are being mastered," he said.
"Many western consultants, financial institutions and marketing specialists are present in the region...it'll be easy to expand in Cuban nickel with low investment costs."
He singled out the 30,000 tonnes a year Las Camariocas nickel refinery, under construction some 20 kilometres from Moa, which was negotiating with potential western partners.
In stainless steel, nickel's prime area of consumption, two Cuban-owned facilities managed by the holding company Acinox had sales of $142.1 million in 1996, written material from Pariser showed.
Designed to produce 150,000 tonnes a year of stainless steel slabs, the Las Tunas plant had so far been mainly producing carbon steel and annual stainless output amounted to just 9,000 tonnes.
Cuban mining has rebounded rapidly in the last few years after being badly hit by the collapse of its main market and technology supplier, the former Soviet bloc.
However, the U.S. Helms-Burton law, introduced in March 1996, seeks to penalise foreign investors in Cuba judged to be "trafficking" in expropriated, formerly U.S.-owned properties.
